stem:
A motorcyclist with left rib fractures is breathing comfortably with oxygen saturation of 97%. CT has shown a small left pneumothorax that has not yet been drained. Paramedics had started a nitrous oxide–oxygen mixture for pain, and the emergency consultant stops it and switches to intravenous opioid analgesia.

Which property of nitrous oxide is the main reason for stopping it?

options.label: A
options.text: Nitrous oxide enters the gas space faster than nitrogen leaves
options.explanation: Nitrous oxide is far more soluble in blood than nitrogen, so it diffuses into an air-filled space much faster than nitrogen can diffuse out. The pneumothorax enlarges and can progress to tension.

options.label: B
options.text: Nitrogen diffuses into the pleural gas faster than it can leave
options.explanation: The direction is reversed. Nitrogen is poorly soluble and leaves the trapped gas slowly; it is nitrous oxide that moves in quickly.

options.label: C
options.text: Nitrous oxide raises pulmonary vascular resistance and pressure
options.explanation: A modest rise in pulmonary vascular resistance can occur, but it does not enlarge a pneumothorax and is not the main reason to stop the gas here.

options.label: D
options.text: Nitrous oxide causes diffusion hypoxia when the mask is removed
options.explanation: Diffusion hypoxia is a real effect at the end of nitrous oxide use and is prevented by giving oxygen. It does not explain the risk to an undrained pneumothorax.

options.label: E
options.text: Nitrous oxide depresses respiratory drive after chest trauma
options.explanation: Nitrous oxide has little effect on respiratory drive at analgesic concentrations. His breathing is comfortable, and the concern is the trapped gas.

context: Nitrous oxide diffuses into trapped gas spaces faster than nitrogen leaves, so it can enlarge an undrained pneumothorax.
